Russian Gas & Water Utilities Rebounded After 2021 Tariff Hike on Equipment Imports

A look back at Russia’s 2021 trade-policy move reveals a notable impact on the nation’s Gas & Water Utilities industry—but also its subsequent stabilization. In June 2021, the Russian government imposed a 20% import tariff on key gas and water infrastructure equipment, including meters, pressure regulators, and filtration units, primarily sourced from European and Asian suppliers. The measure, introduced to support domestic manufacturing, triggered immediate cost increases for utilities and led to project delays across the sector.

PJSC GAZPROM GAZORASPREDELENIYE UFA, one of the affected companies, reported a 12% rise in capital expenditure for the second half of 2021. “The tariff forced us to reassess ongoing pipeline upgrades and postpone non-critical maintenance,” said Dmitry Isayev, Head of Procurement at the company, at the time. “We also accelerated efforts to source from Russian manufacturers, but the transition was not immediate.”

Industry analysts estimate that the tariff added approximately 6.5 billion rubles ($90 million) in aggregate costs for gas and water utilities nationwide during 2021. Anna Sidorova, an energy sector analyst at Novatek Consulting, explained, “Smaller regional utilities were especially hard-hit, as they often lack bargaining power and depend on imported components for safety compliance.”

Despite these challenges, the Russian Association of Utility Companies noted that most firms adapted by mid-2022. “The initial shock was significant, but by late 2021 we observed a sharp rise in domestic equipment orders,” said Association President Sergey Mikhailov. “Several Russian manufacturers ramped up production to fill the supply gap, and the government offered expedited certification for local products.”

While some infrastructure projects experienced temporary setbacks, utility services remained largely uninterrupted. The trade-policy measure did succeed in boosting domestic production, though at the cost of higher short-term expenses and a brief slowdown in modernization programs.

Looking back, most major utilities, including PJSC GAZPROM GAZORASPREDELENIYE UFA, have since restored their investment pipelines. “We weathered the adjustment period and resumed normal operations,” Isayev reflected in a recent statement. “Today, our reliance on local suppliers is higher, which aligns with the government’s long-term strategic goals.”

No further disruptions related to the 2021 tariff hike have been reported.
